text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori arrived in Washington on Saturday after an emergency summit in Toronto with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on the 46-day-old Lima hostage crisis.
Fujimori's plane landed at Andrews Air Force Base outside Washington at 5 p.m. EST (2200 GMT), and was greeted by U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs Jeffrey Davidow.
The two men were due to hold private talks on Saturday evening, but officials said no news briefings were scheduled.
Fujimori is scheduled to meet on Monday with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and other State Department officials to discuss the hostage crisis.
On Sunday, he will hold talks with U.S. Drug Policy Director Gen. Barry McCaffrey and attend a World Bank meeting on loans for small enterprises, Peruvian officials said.

Guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement are holding 72 Peruvian and Japanese officials and businessmen in the Japanese ambassador's mansion, demanding freedom for hundreds of jailed rebels.

Officials in Lima had said they hoped Fujimori could meet President Bill Clinton but the White House said Clinton had taken a low-key posture on the hostage crisis on the advice of his counter-terrorism experts.

In addition to Albright, Fujimori is due to meet Undersecretary of State for Political Affairs Peter Tarnoff and Clinton's longtime adviser and special envoy to Latin America, Thomas "Mack" McLarty, U.S. officials said.
The United States has voiced support for Fujimori's handling of the hostage crisis, praising him publicly for not giving into the rebels' demands.
At Saturday's summit, Fujimori and Hashimoto agreed to push for direct talks with the rebels, even though they ruled out the guerrillas' non-negotiable demand -- freedom for their jailed comrades.

But the leader of the operation, MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa, on Saturday appeared to dash any hopes of a quick settlement, reiterating that rebels would release their captives only after 400 jailed comrades were freed.
